subject: English
summaryPoints: Sentences are classified structurally into four types: simple (one independent clause), compound (two coordinate independent clauses joined by FANBOYS or a semicolon), complex (one independent clause plus one or more dependent clauses), and compound-complex (at least two independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses).

Simple past tense expresses actions completed at a definite time in the past, taking inflectional '-ed/-d' for regular verbs or internal vowel changes for irregular verbs, accompanied by definitive past adverbials (yesterday, ago, last week, in 1995).

Modal verbs express degrees of advice and warning: 'must' and 'have to' convey strong necessity/obligation; 'should' and 'ought to' provide moderate advice; and 'had better' conveys advice carrying an implied warning of negative consequences.

Semicolons join related independent clauses without coordinating conjunctions, or link independent clauses when the second begins with a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, nevertheless, furthermore).
Colons introduce formal lists, direct expansions, or explanatory paraphrases of preceding independent clauses, and separate hours from minutes.

Effective summary writing condenses an original text to approximately one-third of its length in the writer's own words, omitting personal interpretations, extraneous examples, and digressions while preserving core thesis points.

formulas.label: Compound Sentence with Coordinating Conjunction
formulas.expr: Independent Clause + , + Coordinating Conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) + Independent Clause

formulas.label: Semicolon with Conjunctive Adverb Formula
formulas.expr: Independent Clause + ; + conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, nevertheless) + , + Independent Clause

formulas.label: Complex Sentence Structure
formulas.expr: Subordinating Conjunction + Dependent Clause + , + Independent Clause  OR  Independent Clause + Subordinating Conjunction + Dependent Clause

formulas.label: Compound-Complex Sentence Formula
formulas.expr: Independent Clause + Coordinating Conjunction + Independent Clause + Subordinating Conjunction + Dependent Clause

examTip: When punctuating compound sentences with conjunctive adverbs in EUEE items, verify the punctuation: use a semicolon before the conjunctive adverb and a comma after it (e.g., 'Clause 1; however, Clause 2'). Never join two independent clauses with only a comma (avoid comma splices).

keyDefinitions.definition: A sentence containing a single independent clause that expresses a complete thought with a subject and a finite predicate.
A sentence consisting of two or more independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions, semicolons, or conjunctive adverbs.
A sentence composed of one main independent clause linked to one or more dependent subordinate clauses.
A concise, objective synthesis of a text's essential ideas written in the summarizer's own words, representing roughly one-third of the original text.

eueeFocusTopics: Identification of sentence structures (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex)
Punctuation conventions: semicolons vs commas vs colons
Modal verbs for warnings and advice ('must', 'should', 'ought to', 'had better')
Phrasal verbs based on 'fill' ('fill in' for forms, 'fill up' for tanks, 'fill out')
Descriptive adjectives and collocations related to travel and personality
